results.result: The study manipulated brain lateralization in 100 newborn domestic chicks by exposing half to light during embryonic days 18-21 (Li-chicks, strongly lateralized) and incubating the other half in darkness (Di-chicks, weakly lateralized).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C80-C82 describe the experimental manipulation and sample. The light exposure manipulation is well-established in the literature (C59, C63-C66) and the sample sizes are clearly reported. The experimental design is straightforward and adequately described.

results.result: Chicks were trained to select the 4th item in a sagittal array, then tested with the array rotated 90° to create left-right options, under binocular and monocular viewing conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C83-C89 describe the training and testing procedures. The methodology is clearly described with reference to figures showing the apparatus configuration. This paradigm has been used in previous studies (C33-C34), providing validation for the approach.

results.result: Experiment 1 provided reliable spatial and ordinal cues by maintaining constant inter-item distances, while Experiment 2 made spatial information unreliable by varying inter-item distances across trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95 describe the key experimental manipulation distinguishing the two experiments. The manipulation is clearly described and logically designed to test the role of spatial versus ordinal information. The specific distances used are reported (C94).

results.result: In the sagittal test of Experiment 1, Li-chicks (strongly lateralized) showed higher accuracy in selecting the 4th item compared to Di-chicks (weakly lateralized) when both spatial and ordinal cues were available.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C96-C98, and C185 report findings from the sagittal test with statistical support (t(45.1)=3.132, p=0.003, d=0.904; BF=12.588). The effect size is large (d=0.904) and the Bayes Factor provides strong evidence. Both groups selected the 4th item above chance, but Li-chicks were more accurate.

results.result: In the fronto-parallel binocular test of Experiment 1, only strongly lateralized Li-chicks showed a left-to-right bias, selecting the 4th left item significantly more than the 4th right item, while Di-chicks showed no directional preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C99-C105, C140-C142 report the key finding on directional bias. Li-chicks showed strong left bias (t(23)=4.791, p<0.001, d=1.635; BF=337.124) while Di-chicks showed no difference between left and right (t(23)=0.218, p=1.000, d=0.076; BF=0.219). The large effect size and strong Bayes Factor support the conclusion. This is the primary evidence for the main claim about lateralization and directionality.

results.result: In the fronto-parallel monocular left test of Experiment 1 (right hemisphere processing), Li-chicks successfully selected the 4th left item and showed a left bias, while Di-chicks failed to select the correct item.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 report findings from the left monocular test with statistical support. Li-chicks selected 4th left more than 4th right (t(23)=6.056, p<0.001, d=2.088; BF=5598.452) and outperformed Di-chicks (t(45.9)=3.988, p<0.001, d=1.151; BF=104.830). The very large effect sizes and Bayes Factors provide strong evidence.

results.result: In the fronto-parallel monocular right test of Experiment 1 (left hemisphere processing), Li-chicks successfully selected the 4th right item, while Di-chicks failed.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C116 report findings from the right monocular test. Li-chicks selected 4th right more than 4th left (t(23)=-6.151, p<0.001, d=1.844; BF=6887.511) and outperformed Di-chicks (t(44.3)=2.850, p=0.013, d=0.823; BF=6.799). The large effect sizes and strong Bayes Factors support the findings.

results.result: Prenatal light experience stimulates brain development and hemispheric specialization, which enhances spatial-numerical association and performance in ordinal tasks when both spatial and numerical cues are available.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C118 and C138-C139 synthesize the findings from Experiment 1. The conclusion is well-supported by the consistent pattern of results showing Li-chicks outperforming Di-chicks across multiple tests (C98, C104, C105, C109, C115) and showing directional bias (C101, C107).

results.result: In the sagittal test of Experiment 2 (unreliable spatial cues), both Li-chicks and Di-chicks successfully selected the 4th item with no difference in accuracy between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C119-C121 report findings from the sagittal test of Experiment 2. Statistical analysis shows no difference between groups (t(45.8)=0.211, p=1.000, d=0.059; BF=0.283). The very small effect size and Bayes Factor favoring the null hypothesis support the conclusion of no difference.

results.result: In the fronto-parallel binocular test of Experiment 2 (unreliable spatial cues), both Li-chicks and Di-chicks selected both 4th left and right items above chance with no side bias in either group and no difference between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 report the disappearance of the left bias when spatial information is unreliable. Neither Li-chicks (t(25)=1.910, p=0.135, d=0.624; BF=0.997) nor Di-chicks (t(25)=-0.218, p=1.000, d=0.098; BF=0.219) showed directional bias. This contrasts with Experiment 1 and supports the role of spatial information in the bias.

results.result: In the fronto-parallel left monocular test of Experiment 2 (right hemisphere, unreliable spatial cues), both Li-chicks and Di-chicks failed to select the correct item, suggesting the right hemisphere requires spatial information for ordinal tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 report failure of both groups in the left monocular condition when spatial cues are unreliable. Statistical analysis shows no difference between groups for either 4th left (t(49.8)=0.066, p=1.000, d=0.018; BF=0.279) or 4th right (t(49.2)=-0.218, p=1.000, d=0.060; BF=0.284). The interpretation that the right hemisphere relies on spatial information is reasonable given the contrast with Experiment 1.

results.result: In the fronto-parallel monocular right test of Experiment 2 (left hemisphere, unreliable spatial cues), only Li-chicks succeeded in selecting the 4th right item, suggesting the left hemisphere can process ordinal information and that lateralization influences numerical cognition even without spatial information.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C137 report that Li-chicks succeeded (t(25)=-4.946, p<0.001, d=-1.447; BF=573.520) while Di-chicks failed. However, the between-group comparison was not significant (t(49.9)=2.110, p=0.080, d=0.585; BF=1.678). The Bayes Factor of 1.678 is inconclusive. While Li-chicks showed within-group success, the lack of significant between-group difference weakens the claim that lateralization per se is the critical factor. The interpretation requires caution.

results.result: Pre-hatching light stimulation did not affect performance when spatial information was unavailable (Experiment 2), demonstrating that the integration of spatial and numerical processing is fundamental to numerical spatialization and that left-to-right bias depends on spatial information availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C148, C163, and C176 synthesize the key findings from Experiment 2. The disappearance of group differences in the sagittal test (C121) and binocular fronto-parallel test (C123-C124), along with the failure of both groups in the left monocular condition (C127-C128), support the conclusion that spatial information is critical for the lateralization effect on numerical spatialization.

results.result: Brain lateralization is fundamental for developing a left-to-right oriented spatial-numerical association, with the right hemisphere playing a key role in integrating spatial and numerical cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14, C111, C126, C142-C146 state the main conclusions. These are well-supported by the pattern of results: (1) only Li-chicks showed left-to-right bias in Experiment 1 (C101, C103); (2) the bias disappeared when spatial information was unreliable (C123, C125); (3) Li-chicks succeeded in monocular conditions in Experiment 1 but not in left monocular condition of Experiment 2 (C106-C109, C127-C128). The convergent evidence across multiple tests supports the conclusion.

results.result: The right hemisphere is specialized for spatial cue analysis while the left hemisphere is more specialized for processing ordinal information, with left-to-right numerical spatialization based on preferential right hemisphere processing when spatial information is available.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 propose hemispheric specialization for different types of information. The right hemisphere specialization for spatial processing is supported by the failure in left monocular condition of Experiment 2 (C127-C131). However, the evidence for left hemisphere specialization in ordinal processing is weaker, relying primarily on the success of Li-chicks in right monocular condition of Experiment 2 (C132-C137), where the between-group comparison was not significant (C135). The interpretation requires additional evidence.

results.result: Light stimulation enhances the development and specialization of both hemispheres, boosting cognitive performance, with the right hemisphere showing dominance when spatial cues are available.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C191 synthesize findings on the effect of light stimulation. Li-chicks succeeded in both monocular conditions of Experiment 1 while Di-chicks failed (C106-C109, C113-C115, C190). The similarity between binocular and left monocular performance in Li-chicks (C187) suggests right hemisphere dominance when spatial cues are available. The interpretation is supported by citations to previous anatomical work (C192).

results.result: The results support the right-hemisphere dominance model over the emotional valence and BAFT models, as it provides a more comprehensive and parsimonious explanation of numerical spatialization across multiple contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C195-C196 and C202-C205 evaluate the theoretical models. The experimental design specifically tested predictions of the three models (Table 1). The finding that Li-chicks showed a left bias (supporting right-hemisphere model, C56) rather than right bias (emotional valence model, C57) or no bias (BAFT, C58), combined with the dependence on spatial information, supports the right-hemisphere dominance model. The argument is strengthened by citations showing this model accounts for multiple paradigms (C203).

results.result: The left-to-right bias may have evolved as an adaptive strategy for efficient environmental scanning and numerical processing, with lateralization variability within populations representing an evolutionarily stable strategy that maintains fitness through behavioral unpredictability.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C184 present speculative evolutionary interpretations. While these are interesting hypotheses supported by citations to relevant concepts (bet-hedging C181-C182, behavioral unpredictability C183, evolutionarily stable strategy C184), they are explicitly speculative (C166 uses 'can speculate', C167 'may have', C171 'might have'). The experimental data do not directly test these evolutionary hypotheses. These remain plausible interpretations requiring future empirical validation.

results.result: In Experiment 1 (with reliable spatial cues), strongly lateralized (Li) chicks showed a left-to-right bias in numerical spatialization, selecting the 4th left item preferentially in binocular tests, while weakly lateralized (Di) chicks showed no directional bias. Li-chicks also outperformed Di-chicks in accuracy. This demonstrates that brain lateralization is fundamental for developing left-to-right oriented spatial-numerical associations.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers affirm this core finding. The editor states the study 'demonstrates how a left-right bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralization' with 'compelling' evidence. Reviewer 1 confirms 'the authors are successful in revealing that the lateralized brain is advantageous in the number sense' and that 'the left-to-right numerical representation appeared when the distance between items gave a reliable spatial cue.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges this as 'the first study to show how a L-R bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralisation.' No reviewer challenges these findings.

results.result: In Experiment 2 (with unreliable spatial cues), the left-to-right bias disappeared in both Li and Di chicks during binocular testing, and Li-chicks did not outperform Di-chicks. This demonstrates that spatial information is essential for the expression of directional numerical spatialization.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes that 'the left-to-right numerical representation appeared when the distance between items gave a reliable spatial cue,' implicitly acknowledging that without reliable spatial cues (Experiment 2), the bias did not appear. The editor and other reviewers do not challenge these findings. The contrast between Experiments 1 and 2 is central to the study's logic and is accepted by reviewers.

results.result: In monocular tests of Experiment 1, Li-chicks succeeded in selecting the 4th item when using either the left eye (right hemisphere) or right eye (left hemisphere), while Di-chicks failed in both conditions. This demonstrates that light-induced lateralization enhances cognitive performance in both hemispheres and supports the right hemisphere's role in spatial-numerical integration.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough to support their arguments' and notes the importance of 'light-exposure induced lateralization' for the findings. The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling.' No reviewer questions the monocular test results or their interpretation regarding hemispheric contributions. The findings are treated as supporting evidence for the main conclusions.

results.result: In the left eye/right hemisphere monocular condition of Experiment 2 (unreliable spatial cues), both Li and Di chicks failed to select the 4th item, indicating that the right hemisphere cannot process ordinal information alone without spatial cues. This suggests ordinality is not lateralized to the right hemisphere.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. The pattern of results across monocular conditions in both experiments is accepted as part of the overall evidence. Reviewer 1's statement that 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough to support their arguments' encompasses these monocular findings. The interpretation about right hemisphere limitations is consistent with the reviewers' acceptance of the spatial-dependence of the effect.

results.result: In the right eye/left hemisphere monocular condition of Experiment 2, Li-chicks succeeded in selecting the 4th item even without reliable spatial cues, while Di-chicks failed. This suggests the left hemisphere is more specialized for processing ordinal information and that lateralization influences numerical cognition even without spatial information.
results.evaluation: This finding is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is part of the overall behavioral evidence that Reviewer 1 describes as 'strong enough to support their arguments.' The contrast between left and right hemisphere performance in Experiment 2 supports the hemispheric specialization claims that all reviewers accept. No reviewer challenges the interpretation of left hemisphere involvement in ordinal processing.

results.result: The right hemisphere plays a key role in integrating spatial and numerical cues, being specialized for both spatial and numerical information processing. The integration of spatial and numerical processing within shared cortical regions is fundamental to numerical spatialization, with hemispheric specialization and environmental stimulation jointly contributing.
results.evaluation: The editor states the study 'demonstrates how a left-right bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralization.' Reviewer 1 notes the study reveals 'that the lateralized brain is advantageous in the number sense, in which numerosity is associated with spatial arrangements of items.' Reviewer 1 also states 'Specification of the responsible neural substrates in the presumed right hemisphere is expected in future research,' acknowledging the right hemisphere's role as established by the current findings. All reviewers accept the hemispheric specialization framework.

results.result: Higher levels of brain lateralization enhance cognitive performance generally and specifically boost numerical abilities. Li-chicks outperformed Di-chicks in the sagittal test and monocular conditions, demonstrating that prenatal light experience stimulates brain development and hemispheric specialization, which enhances performance in spatial/numerical tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the authors are successful in revealing that the lateralized brain is advantageous in the number sense' and notes 'it remains largely speculative as to whether the lateralized brains have a cognitive gain or a sort of fitness advantage' but that 'In the present study...the authors are successful in revealing' this advantage. The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling.' The performance advantage of Li-chicks is central to the study's conclusions and is accepted by all reviewers.

results.result: Background claims about the Mental Number Line (MNL) in humans, including its traditional characterization as left-to-right and culturally rooted, and evidence showing inconsistency across paradigms and reading directions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 extensively challenges the framing around the 'Mental Number Line' terminology and the characterization of human numerical spatialization. The reviewer states 'I would query the way the experiment was contextualised' and notes 'they seem to be asserting that humans have a left-to-right (L-R) MNL. This is highly contentious.' The reviewer points out that 'evidence remains inconsistent across paradigms' and cites studies showing no L-R bias in humans. The reviewer requests the paper 'should be shorn of its misleading contextualisation, including the term "Mental Number Line."' After revision, the reviewer notes 'The background and terminology in the text have been significantly altered and clarified: Spatial Numerical Association (SNA) instead of Mental Number Line (MNL),' indicating the authors addressed these concerns by reframing the claims.

results.result: Spatial-numerical associations (SNA) have been reported in newborns, infants, and nonhuman animals, suggesting neural/innate origins and challenging the predominant role of culture. Nervous systems across species are prewired for relating numbers to space, though numerical spatialization remains flexible and subject to modulation by experience.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a conceptual challenge: 'their clever experiment shows that an experimental manipulation creates the bias. If it were innate and common to other species, the experimental manipulation shouldn't matter. There would always be a L-R bias.' This questions whether the findings truly demonstrate innateness versus developmental plasticity. However, after revision, Reviewer 2 acknowledges the authors 'make important arguments for the evolutionary advantage of the bias' and accepts the study should be published. The tension between innate predisposition and developmental modulation remains somewhat unresolved in the reviewers' comments, though the overall framework is accepted.

results.result: Various theoretical accounts link SNA to brain lateralization but previously lacked direct experimental evidence. The biological mechanisms and neural underpinnings of SNA were largely unknown, and no research had directly investigated the effect of hemispheric specialization on number spatialization through direct manipulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges this as 'the first study to show how a L-R bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralisation' and praises the 'Novel methodology for investigating the innateness and neural basis of a L-R bias.' Reviewer 1 notes 'it remains largely speculative as to whether the lateralized brains have a cognitive gain' before this study. The novelty and importance of directly testing lateralization's role is affirmed by all reviewers.

results.result: The experimental manipulation: lateralization levels in domestic chicks can be manipulated by controlling light exposure during embryonic days 18-21. Light exposure leads to asymmetrical stimulation creating strongly lateralized (Li) chicks, while dark incubation prevents lateralization creating weakly lateralized (Di) chicks.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes 'Brain lateralization was manipulated by light exposure during the terminal phase of incubation' and states 'The light-exposure induced lateralization, though quite unique in avian species, together with the lack of intense inter-hemispheric direct connections...was critical for the successful analysis in this study.' All reviewers accept this manipulation as valid and well-established. No concerns are raised about the methodology for creating lateralized vs. non-lateralized groups.

results.result: Methodological details: 100 chicks were tested across two experiments using an ordinal task where chicks learned to select the 4th item in a sagittal array, then were tested with the array rotated 90° in various viewing conditions (binocular, monocular left, monocular right). Experiment 1 had reliable spatial cues; Experiment 2 had unreliable spatial cues.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough to support their arguments' and describes the methodology approvingly. Reviewer 2 praises the 'Novel methodology for investigating the innateness and neural basis of a L-R bias.' No reviewer raises methodological concerns about the experimental design, sample size, or procedures. The methods are treated as sound and appropriate for testing the hypotheses.

results.result: Theoretical models (right-hemisphere dominance, emotional valence, BAFT) all acknowledge hemispheric specialization's role in SNA but make different predictions. The right-hemisphere dominance model provides the most comprehensive and parsimonious explanation, accounting for behavior across multiple contexts including both ordinal and magnitude comparison tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the theoretical framework or the authors' evaluation of competing models. Reviewer 1 notes 'Specification of the responsible neural substrates in the presumed right hemisphere is expected in future research,' accepting the right hemisphere framework. The theoretical discussion is treated as appropriate contextualization rather than a primary empirical claim requiring validation. No reviewer disputes the authors' theoretical synthesis.

results.result: Speculative evolutionary and ecological interpretations: establishing a left-biased anchor point may have evolutionary advantages for environmental scanning and numerical processing; lateralization variability may represent adaptive bet-hedging; the left-to-right bias may have evolved from scanning behaviors and been assimilated into numerical cognition.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 initially states 'The authors also speculate, usefully, on why chicks and other species might have a L-R bias. I don't think the speculations are convincing, but at least if there is an evolutionary basis for the bias, it should at least be discussed.' After revision, Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors take on this challenge and make important arguments for the evolutionary advantage of the bias is (see lines 138ff, 375ff, 444ff), though this is likely still to be controversial.' This indicates the speculations are viewed as useful but not definitively established—they remain open questions rather than supported conclusions.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate evolutionary speculation claims (C166-C184). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting claims are 'explicitly speculative' and 'remain plausible interpretations requiring future empirical validation.' Peer review also rates UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 2 finding speculations 'useful' but 'not convincing' initially, later noting they remain 'likely still to be controversial.' Both agree these are open questions rather than established conclusions.

Both address right monocular test in Experiment 2 (C132-C137). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to non-significant between-group comparison (BF=1.678) despite Li-chicks' within-group success, noting 'interpretation requires caution.' Peer review rates SUPPORTED, accepting this as part of overall behavioral evidence and hemispheric specialization framework. Peer reviewers do not explicitly discuss the statistical ambiguity that concerns OpenEval.

Both evaluate core directional bias findings from Experiment 1 (C12, C99-C105, C140-C142). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with strong statistical evidence (large effect sizes, BF=337.124 for Li-chicks' left bias). Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with all reviewers affirming this as 'compelling' evidence and the 'core finding.' Complete agreement on this central result.

Both address left monocular test failure in Experiment 2 (C127-C131). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting statistical evidence shows no group differences and interpreting this as right hemisphere reliance on spatial information. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, accepting this pattern as part of overall evidence without challenge. Both agree on the finding and its interpretation regarding right hemisphere limitations.

Both evaluate disappearance of directional bias in Experiment 2 (C11, C121-C125, C147). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on statistical evidence showing no bias in either group when spatial cues unreliable. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 acknowledging bias appeared only 'when the distance between items gave a reliable spatial cue.' Both agree this contrast with Experiment 1 is central to the study's logic.

Both address experimental methodology (C6-C9, C83-C95). OpenEval rates training/testing procedures as SUPPORTED, noting clear description and validation from previous studies. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 stating 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough' and Reviewer 2 praising 'Novel methodology.' Both accept the experimental design as sound.

OpenEval R1 addresses experimental manipulation and sample (C6-C7, C80-C82). Peer R11 addresses light exposure manipulation (C59-C68, C81-C82). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes manipulation is 'well-established in the literature.' Peer review confirms 'light-exposure induced lateralization' was 'critical for the successful analysis' and accepts it as valid. Both agree on the validity of the lateralization manipulation.

Both address left monocular test in Experiment 1 (C106-C110). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with very strong statistical evidence (BF=5598.452, d=2.088). Peer review also rates SUPPORTED as part of monocular findings that contribute to 'compelling' evidence. Both agree these results support the hemispheric contribution claims.

OpenEval R7 addresses right monocular test in Experiment 1 (C113-C116). Peer R3 includes these claims (C113-C116) along with other monocular findings. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval cites strong statistical evidence (BF=6887.511). Peer review accepts monocular results as supporting hemispheric contributions. Both agree on the validity of these findings.

OpenEval R16 synthesizes light stimulation effects (C186-C191). Peer R3 includes some overlapping claims about monocular performance. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes Li-chicks' success in monocular conditions suggesting right hemisphere dominance. Peer review accepts light-exposure lateralization as important for the findings. Both agree on the role of lateralization.

OpenEval R4 addresses sagittal test findings (C10, C96-C98, C185). Peer R1 includes C10, C98 among broader core findings. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes large effect size (d=0.904) and strong BF. Peer review accepts this as part of 'compelling' evidence for main conclusions. Both agree on the validity of these results.

OpenEval R14 synthesizes main conclusions (C13-C14, C111, C126, C142-C146). Peer R1 includes overlapping claims (C14, C142-C146) in core findings. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes 'convergent evidence across multiple tests.' Peer review describes evidence as 'compelling' with all reviewers affirming core findings. Complete agreement on main conclusions.

Both address main conclusions about lateralization and spatial-numerical associations (C13, C111, C126). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on convergent evidence. Peer R6 also rates SUPPORTED, with editor and reviewers affirming the study 'demonstrates how a left-right bias...depends on brain lateralization.' Both agree on the core theoretical conclusions.

Both address hemispheric specialization claims (C161-C163). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting right hemisphere evidence is stronger while left hemisphere evidence relies on non-significant between-group comparison. Peer R6 rates SUPPORTED, accepting hemispheric specialization framework without noting statistical limitations. Peer reviewers are more accepting of the hemispheric specialization interpretation than OpenEval.

Both evaluate theoretical model comparisons (C195-C196, C202-C205). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting experimental design tested model predictions and findings support right-hemisphere dominance model. Peer R13 also rates SUPPORTED, accepting theoretical framework as appropriate contextualization. Both agree the theoretical synthesis is well-grounded in the data.

OpenEval R8 synthesizes Experiment 1 findings (C117-C118, C138-C139). Peer R7 addresses performance advantage of lateralized brains (includes C117-C118). Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes consistent pattern across tests. Peer review confirms authors 'are successful in revealing that the lateralized brain is advantageous.' Both agree on the synthesis of Experiment 1 results.

OpenEval R9 addresses sagittal test in Experiment 2 (C11, C119-C121). Peer R2 includes C11, C121 among claims about spatial cue dependence. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes very small effect size and BF favoring null. Peer review accepts this as part of the contrast between experiments. Both agree on the finding of no group difference.

OpenEval R13 synthesizes Experiment 2 key findings (C147-C148, C163, C176). Peer R2 includes C147 among claims about spatial cue dependence. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes disappearance of effects when spatial information unreliable. Peer review accepts this contrast as central to study logic. Both agree on the interpretation of Experiment 2 results.

OpenEval R3 addresses experimental manipulation distinguishing the two experiments (C90-C95). Peer R12 includes these claims in overall methodology evaluation. Both rate SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes manipulation is 'clearly described and logically designed.' Peer review accepts methodology as sound. Both agree on the validity of the experimental design.

Peer R8 addresses framing around 'Mental Number Line' terminology and human numerical spatialization (C1-C4, C17-C24). Rated UNCERTAIN by peer reviewers, with Reviewer 2 extensively challenging the framing as 'highly contentious' and requesting terminology changes. No corresponding OpenEval result directly addresses these background/framing claims. Peer reviewers identified concerns about contextualization that OpenEval did not separately evaluate.

Peer R9 addresses claims about innateness versus developmental plasticity (C3-C4, C25-C30). Rated UNCERTAIN by peer reviewers, with Reviewer 2 questioning whether findings demonstrate innateness given that experimental manipulation matters. No corresponding OpenEval result directly addresses these conceptual claims about innateness. Peer reviewers raised theoretical concerns about the innate/developmental distinction that OpenEval did not separately evaluate.

Peer R10 addresses novelty claims about being first to test lateralization's role (C5, C41, C52-C54). Rated SUPPORTED by peer reviewers who acknowledge this as 'the first study' with 'Novel methodology.' No corresponding OpenEval result directly addresses these novelty/contribution claims. Peer reviewers explicitly evaluated the study's novel contribution, which OpenEval did not separately assess.
